title: About CIA Part 2
description: What CIA Part 2 looks like, who sits it, how to read its questions as the internal auditor running an engagement, how to pace and prepare, how to book it, and how passing fits into becoming certified. Written in plain language by KaiSip from The IIA's published information.
disclaimer: Certified Internal Auditor® and CIA® are registered trademarks, and Global Internal Audit Standards™ is a trademark, of The IIA (The Institute of Internal Auditors, Inc.). KaiSip is an independent study aid. It is not affiliated with, sponsored, endorsed or licensed by The IIA. All notes and questions are written by KaiSip; none are actual exam questions. The IIA alone sets the exam rules and decides eligibility and certification. No study app can promise a pass, including this one.
check_before_booking: Fees, dates, languages and rules on this page were checked on the date shown. They can change, so check theiia.org before you book.

sections.title: The exam at a glance
sections.summary: CIA Part 2, Internal Audit Engagement, is 100 multiple-choice questions in 120 minutes, taken on a computer at a Pearson VUE test center. A scaled score of 600 or higher passes.
items: 100 multiple-choice questions in 120 minutes: 1.2 minutes, or 72 seconds, a question on average.
The IIA's published sample questions each have four options, A to D. KaiSip's practice questions use the same shape, with one best answer.

Part 2 is one of the three CIA exam parts. It is about a single engagement: planning it, gathering and judging evidence, reaching findings and a conclusion, and supervising and communicating while the work is under way.
Reporting the final results and monitoring what management does next belong to Part 3, whose Section D is Engagement Results and Monitoring.
Scores are reported on a scale from 250 to 750, and 600 or higher passes. 600 is a point on that scale, not a percent of the questions.
Wrong answers are not penalized, so answer every question, including the ones you are unsure of.
No breaks are scheduled. You may step away, but the clock keeps running.
You sit the exam in person at a Pearson VUE test center. The IIA ended online testing on 27 May 2025.
The exam is non-disclosed: The IIA does not publish current questions and answers. Every KaiSip question is written by KaiSip, and none is a real exam question.
Part 2 rests on the Global Internal Audit Standards, published on 9 January 2024 and effective from 9 January 2025.

sections.title: What Part 2 is and who sits it
sections.summary: Part 2 is for candidates on the three-part CIA route. You can sit it before your work experience is complete, and in any order with the other two parts.
items: Entry to the three-part CIA route: a degree, or an active Internal Audit Practitioner (IAP) designation. You may sit the exams before your internal audit experience is complete; the experience is needed to be certified, not to test.
An active IAP holder gets a waiver for Part 1, the exam they already passed as the IAP exam, and sits Parts 2 and 3 only.

The IIA does not prescribe an order for the three parts. KaiSip's view: Part 2 applies Part 1's rules on independence, objectivity, risk and control inside one engagement, so those rules are worth having first.

Your seat in Part 2: the internal auditor running an engagement, under an engagement supervisor. You plan, test, conclude and communicate; the chief audit executive, or a supervisor they delegate to, approves.
The CIA program must be completed within 3 years of approval.

sections.title: The three sections and their weights
sections.summary: The IIA's syllabus splits Part 2 into three sections. A section's weight is its share of the exam, so it is a fair guide to where your study time goes.
items: Section A, Engagement Planning, is half the exam at 50%. It runs from objectives, scope and criteria through the engagement risk assessment to the approach, the work program and the resources the work needs.

Section B, Information Gathering, Analysis, and Evaluation, is 40%: sources and quality of evidence, audit technology and analytics, findings and their significance, workpapers and the engagement conclusion.
Section C, Engagement Supervision and Communication, is the smallest at 10%, about one question in ten. It covers supervising the work and communicating while the engagement is under way.
Sections A and B together are 90% of the exam, so most of your review time goes there.
The syllabus lists 17 numbered topics: 7 in Section A, 8 in B and 2 in C. KaiSip's notes use matching codes, so 2A6 is Part 2, Section A, topic 6.

sections.title: What the syllabus verbs tell you
sections.summary: The syllabus gives no depth label for a topic. Each topic line starts with a verb, and that verb signals how deep its questions can go. The three groups below are KaiSip's reading.
items: Know it (Identify): 1 of Part 2's 17 topics, the sources of engagement information. Expect to pick the method or document that fits a given objective.
Use it (Apply): 4 topics: analytical approaches and process mapping, analytical review, supervision and communication. Expect a situation and the question of how to handle it well.

Weigh and decide (Determine, Evaluate, Plan, Complete, Prepare, Summarize): 12 topics, among them objectives and scope, criteria, the risk assessment, the approach, the work program, resources, evidence quality, findings, workpapers and conclusions. Expect several reasonable moves and one that fits best.
In proportion, Part 2 has far more weigh-and-decide topics than Part 1. Practice until you can say why the closest wrong choice loses.

The IT, cybersecurity, continuity, finance and business-process lines in topic 2A3 are at recognize level. Spot the risk and the kind of control a plan must cover; you are not asked to configure or calculate like a specialist.

sections.title: Syllabus, languages and Topical Requirements
sections.summary: KaiSip teaches the current syllabus and the 2024 Standards. Two languages were still on the older syllabus when this page was checked, so confirm which one your exam date uses.
items: The current syllabus was live in English by July 2025. Older books and many free notes still teach the earlier exam and its vocabulary; KaiSip does not.

The three-part exam is offered in 15 languages: English; Arabic; Simplified and Traditional Chinese; French, German, Polish, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish and Turkish; Japanese, Korean, Thai and Vietnamese.
Caution for Arabic: candidates sit the older 2019 syllabus through 27 December 2026 and move to the current one on 28 December 2026.
Caution for Simplified Chinese (mainland China only): it was still on the older 2019 syllabus when checked, and it moves to the current one during the December 2026 testing window.
If either caution applies to you, confirm with The IIA which syllabus your exam date uses before you rely on this course.

Three Part 2 topics, 2A1, 2A3 and 2A5, ask you to recognize how a Topical Requirement applies while planning. For assurance work on its topic, conformance is required; for advisory work it is recommended, and any exclusion is recorded with a reason.
Topical Requirements enter the exam on dates. Scored questions on a new one do not appear until at least 6 months after it takes effect.

Cybersecurity is testable now. When checked, The IIA's exam reference list also named Third-Party from March 2027, Organizational Behavior from June 2027 and Organizational Resilience from October 2027. The reference list sets which ones the exam tests.
A fifth, Anti-Corruption, was issued on 23 November 2026 and takes effect on 23 November 2027. No exam month was published for it when checked.

sections.title: Read each question as the engagement auditor
sections.summary: A short routine for every question: find what is asked, where the engagement stands and who is acting, check the strength of the rule, then eliminate and choose. These are KaiSip's habits, built on the Standards.
steps: Read the last line first. Note what is asked for: an action, a person, a document, a test or a reason.
Place the question in the engagement: planning, fieldwork, concluding or communicating. The right move depends on the stage, and many wrong options belong to another stage.
Find the actor: the internal auditor, the engagement supervisor, the chief audit executive, the management of the activity under review, senior management or the board.

Find the priority word, such as “first”, “best”, “most” or “most likely”, written in lowercase, and check the strength: does the question ask what is required (a must) or what is good practice (a should)?
Rule out the options topic knowledge eliminates, often two. Settle the last two by asking what comes first, who approves, and whether another competent auditor would accept the evidence.
Say in one sentence why your choice beats the closest wrong choice. Then answer and move on.
items: The order of an engagement is the backbone of Part 2: understand the activity, assess its risks, set objectives, scope and criteria, approve the work program, then test. With “first”, an option from a later step usually loses.

The internal auditor plans, tests, concludes and communicates. The chief audit executive, or an engagement supervisor they delegate to, approves the objectives and scope, the work program and any change to them.

The management of the activity owns the process, the controls and the actions. They give input to the scope and agree action plans; they do not set the scope of an assurance engagement or decide its conclusion.
Evidence is enough when another informed, competent person could repeat the work and reach the same result, not when you feel sure. An interview alone rarely proves that a control operates.
Not the IT specialist, not the external auditor, not the manager. Configuring a system, giving an opinion on the financial statements and fixing the problem are other people's jobs in a CIA question.

“Primary” asks for the main purpose and “most likely” for probability, not severity. CIA questions usually ask for the right answer; if you meet “least”, flip the test. The full list of priority words is on the final review week's cheat sheet.

sections.title: Who acts at each engagement step
sections.summary: Many Part 2 questions turn on who does what, and when, at one step of the engagement. These are KaiSip's patterns, built on the Standards for planning and performing engagements.
items: Objectives and scope: for assurance, the internal auditor sets them with management's input; for advisory work, they are agreed with the party who asked. The chief audit executive or a delegated supervisor approves them (Standard 13.3).

Criteria: if the board and senior management have set adequate criteria, the internal auditor must use them. If not, better ones are worked out with senior management, the board or both (Standard 13.4).
The criteria for each objective are named in the work program, so they are settled before testing, and a later change goes through the work program's approval (Standard 13.6).
Work program: documented and approved before fieldwork starts, and every later change approved promptly (Standard 13.6). Agile or remote work changes when and where the work happens, not this rule.
A change of dates alone, with the objectives, scope and work program unchanged, needs no approval: tell management promptly (Standard 13.1).
A change of objectives or scope during the work: approval first, then timely word to management. Never widen or trim the work quietly, and never leave the news for the final report.

Resources short: the internal auditor raises it with the chief audit executive. A smaller scope is an approved change, and a constraint that stays unresolved is a scope limitation. Only the chief audit executive takes it to the board.
Blocked access: discuss the scope limitation with the management of the activity first. If it stays unresolved, the chief audit executive elevates it to the board.
Evidence and findings: compare the condition with the criteria, identify the root cause with management where possible, and weigh significance by likelihood and impact (Standards 14.1 to 14.3).

Supervision runs from planning to sign-off. Before results go out, the supervisor checks that the workpapers support them and asks for more evidence rather than rewriting a conclusion (Standard 12.3).
An issue that needs immediate attention is raised during the engagement, while management can still act. It is never saved for the final communication.

sections.title: Common traps by section
sections.summary: Each section has a few traps that catch prepared candidates. Most skip a step, move an approval to the wrong person, or treat a statement as proof. These are KaiSip's patterns, organized by The IIA's sections.
items: Planning: letting the management of the activity set the scope of an assurance engagement, or dropping a Topical Requirement because management would prefer it. The internal auditor decides and records the reason for any exclusion.
Planning: reusing last cycle's engagement risk assessment unchanged. A review and update is the minimum, because change in people, systems or structure can add or re-rank risks.
Planning: ranking risks by how easy they are to test. Priority follows impact and likelihood, and fraud risk is part of every engagement risk assessment.

Planning: sampling how a control operates without ever asking whether its design could work. Design is often judged during planning, and the Standards also allow judging it alongside the operating tests; faithful performance of a flawed design proves little.
Planning: starting fieldwork while the work program waits for approval, or cutting steps quietly when time runs short.
Evidence: treating an interview or a self-assessment survey as proof that a control operates. Statements describe; inspection, observation, reperformance and data show.
Evidence: rating a report from the activity's own manager as highly as an extract the internal auditor ran. Reliability comes from independence, corroboration and a well-controlled source, not rank.
Analysis: reporting a variance or an analytics flag as a finding. It is a lead until follow-up shows a gap against the criteria.
Findings: calling the symptom the root cause, or judging significance by money alone. A small amount can matter because of its nature, recurrence or legal effect.

Conclusions: offering a list of findings as the conclusion, or leaving the conclusion out when nothing was found. An assurance conclusion says how effective the processes are, including when they work.
Supervision and communication: one review at the very end, or a supervisor rewriting a conclusion without asking for evidence. An urgent issue waits for no report.

sections.title: Pacing your 120 minutes
sections.summary: 120 minutes for 100 questions is 1.2 minutes each. Use that number to set two checkpoints, not to time every question.
items: Checkpoints: reach question 50 by minute 60; reach question 75 by minute 90. Look at the clock at those two points and otherwise leave it alone.
Ahead at a checkpoint? The minutes you have saved are your review time. Behind? Decide a little faster on the next few questions instead of rushing all of them.
If a question stalls you, choose your best answer and move on. Wrong answers are not penalized, so a best guess beats a blank.
No breaks are scheduled, and the clock keeps running if you take one. Plan as if you will sit straight through.
Part 2 has many short engagement scenarios. A long scenario takes more than the average and a plain rule question takes less, so judge your pace at the checkpoints, never on one question.

sections.title: Your score and KaiSip's numbers
sections.summary: The IIA reports a scaled score. KaiSip never shows one: it shows the percent you got right, by section, and its own readiness band. The two are different things.
items: The IIA converts your raw score to a reporting scale that runs from 250 to 750. A scaled score of 600 or higher passes.
600 is a point on that scale, not a percent of the questions. KaiSip knows of no published way to turn a percent correct into a scaled score, and it does not try.
If you pass, your score report shows no number at all. If you do not, it shows your score and the syllabus areas that need improvement.
A KaiSip mock result shows your percent correct for each section and your pace against the checkpoints. It is labeled as KaiSip's, and it is not The IIA's score.
KaiSip's readiness band is its own summary of your practice. It is a study signal, not a prediction of your result.
A good use of a practice percent: compare your three sections with each other and with last week, and give time to the section furthest behind its weight.

sections.title: Your last week before the exam
sections.summary: A calm seven-day plan with nothing new in it: one full timed mock early, then your slips, the section sheets and the close pairs, and rest at the end.
steps: Seven days out: sit one full timed mock of 100 questions in 120 minutes, using the two checkpoints. This is your last full mock before the exam.
Six days out: review each miss and name the thinking slip behind it. Then recall Section A, half the exam, from memory and check the sheet. Stop at about 90 minutes.
Five days out: the three close pairs (approve or tell, design or operation, symptom or cause), then Section B and a short untimed set in your weakest section.
Four days out: one short timed mock. Then recall the order of planning, what makes evidence enough, and who may staff an engagement.
Three days out: Section C from the engagement auditor's seat, then the principles on speaking up and on reading the question. No timed tests from today on.
Two days out: light review. Say the priority words and the answering routine from memory, then check. Confirm your appointment, ID and route.
One day out: rest. Glance at your own short list of rules, get ready for the morning, and sleep at your usual time.
items: Nothing new this week. The plan sharpens what you already know; a topic you have never studied is better left alone now.
Missed a day? Skip it and carry on with the next one. Never double up.
Recall beats rereading: answer from memory first, then check.
Practice results in any study app, including KaiSip, are not The IIA's scaled scores and cannot predict your result.

sections.title: Registering and fees
sections.summary: You apply to the CIA program once, register for Part 2, then book a seat at a Pearson VUE test center. The IIA's prices change on 4 January 2027.
steps: Check that you meet the entry rule for the three-part route: a degree, or an active Internal Audit Practitioner (IAP) designation.
Apply to the CIA program and pay the application fee, if you have not already done so for another part. Once you are approved, you have 3 years to complete the program.
Register for Part 2 and pay the exam fee. A registration lasts 180 days, unless your program expires sooner.
Book your appointment at a Pearson VUE test center inside that window.
items: Until 3 January 2027: application fee US$120 for IIA members and US$240 for non-members; Part 2 exam fee US$280 for members and US$415 for non-members.
From 4 January 2027: application fee US$145 for members and US$195 for non-members; Part 2 exam fee US$325 for members and US$435 for non-members.
These are The IIA's listed prices for the United States, Canada and some other countries. Where a national institute of The IIA runs the exams, prices may differ.
Fees are not refunded and cannot be transferred.
Need more time? On the three-part route you can buy one 75-day extension of an exam registration for US$100, and one 12-month extension of the program for US$275.
You can change an appointment up to 48 hours before it. Pearson VUE charges US$75 each time.

sections.title: Test center only
sections.summary: The exam is taken in person, on a computer, at a Pearson VUE test center. The IIA ended online testing on 27 May 2025.
items: There is no at-home or online option. Advice that mentions remote testing for this exam is out of date.
Choose a test center and a time of day that suit you, and book early enough to get both. Your appointment must fall inside your 180-day registration.
You can move the appointment up to 48 hours before it, for a Pearson VUE fee of US$75 each time.
The check-in, ID and test-room rules are for The IIA and Pearson VUE to set. Read them in the current candidate handbook and in your appointment confirmation; KaiSip does not restate them.
Plan the trip ahead: know the route, the travel time and a backup, so nothing about the morning is left to chance.

sections.title: Exam day
sections.summary: Arrive with time in hand, pace by your two checkpoints, and answer every question.
items: Bring what The IIA's candidate handbook and your appointment confirmation tell you to bring. Check the ID rules a few days ahead, while there is still time to fix a problem.
100 questions in 120 minutes. Checkpoints: question 50 by minute 60; question 75 by minute 90.
No breaks are scheduled. If you take one, the clock keeps running.
Answer every question. Wrong answers are not penalized, so a best guess always beats a blank.
For each question: read the last line, place the engagement stage, find the actor and the priority word, rule out two options, then settle the final two with a principle.
If your mind goes blank, breathe out slowly, pick your best answer for now and return to it if time allows.

sections.title: After the exam
sections.summary: You do not see a score when you finish. The official result arrives within 3 weeks of your exam date.
items: No immediate unofficial score is shown. Official results arrive within 3 weeks of the exam date.
A pass report shows no numeric score. A report for an exam that was not passed shows the score and the syllabus areas that need improvement.
If you did not pass, you can sit again no sooner than 30 days after your last attempt.
An exam may be taken at most eight times during your program eligibility window, and the program's 3-year clock keeps running.
Treat a report that lists areas to improve as a study map: start with the areas it names, then compare them with your KaiSip section percents.
Passing Part 2 is one step. The other parts you still need, and the experience requirement, stand between you and the CIA.

sections.title: Becoming certified
sections.summary: Passing Part 2 does not make you a Certified Internal Auditor. You also pass the other parts and show internal audit experience. The IIA decides every application.
steps: Pass all three parts within 3 years of your program approval, or Parts 2 and 3 if you hold an active Internal Audit Practitioner (IAP) designation. The IIA does not prescribe the order.
Show internal audit experience: 1 year with a master's degree, or 2 years with a bachelor's degree.
Or, as an active IAP holder, show 5 years of experience. An IAP holder who also has a degree needs the 1 or 2 years that go with that degree.
items: You may sit the exams before the experience is complete. The experience is needed to be certified, not to test.
The IIA's CIA page adds that 2 of an IAP holder's 5 years must fall within the past 3 years.
The candidate handbook also lists a route with 5 years of experience and no degree, but the CIA page showed no such route when checked. If you plan to rely on it, confirm with The IIA first.
KaiSip has not checked the rules for keeping the certification once you hold it. Read them on The IIA's site when you get there.
